text: Once an incident crosses team boundaries, the hard part stops being the technical fix and starts being coordination itself. Get that wrong and you can have three capable teams all actively working the same outage and still move slower than if only one team had responded — because none of them knows what the others have already found, or already ruled out.

Here's the default failure mode, and it's genuinely the default, not an edge case: payments sees elevated errors and starts investigating on their own. Database sees replication lag and starts investigating on their own. Platform sees load balancer errors and does the same. Twenty minutes in, three teams have each spent that time rediscovering the same symptom from a different angle, instead of spending it testing three different hypotheses — because paging is service-scoped by default, and nothing connects the responses together unless something deliberately does.

The fix every mature incident process converges on is one shared channel and one bridge call, the moment an incident goes multi-team — a single source of truth where the IC, the Scribe, and every responding team post findings as they happen. The highest-leverage habit inside that channel is a pinned note of the current hypothesis and what's already been ruled out, so the database team never re-tests a theory payments already disproved ten minutes earlier.

Escalation works the same way: the IC pages exactly the team the current evidence points to, through a defined on-call policy, not by hunting for a phone number mid-incident — and pages further only as the hypothesis changes, because paging every adjacent team just in case floods the channel with people who have nothing to contribute yet. Ownership gets assigned out loud, too, so nobody assumes someone else already has it covered.

A genuine major incident touching a dozen teams scales the same idea with more layers — sub-leads reporting into the IC, a continuous bridge call, and timeboxed status check-ins every fifteen to thirty minutes. The mechanism never changes: one source of truth, explicit ownership, controlled escalation. Next lesson turns to what gets communicated outward, to customers and stakeholders, while all of this is happening.
